index.subtitle: Five worked problems, each pitched at the round it is actually asked in.
index.html:
In one paragraph

Five worked system-design case studies, each written for the round it is actually asked in. Parking lot and elevator are machine-coding problems judged on extensibility, so they lead with class models and concurrency. BookMyShow is asked both ways and gets both. URL shortener and flash sale are boxes-and-arrows rounds, so they lead with capacity math and the read path. Every note follows the same thirteen-section spine — clarifying questions, requirements, architecture, decisions with the rejected alternative named, failure modes, and a rehearsed thirty-second spoken opener.

How they connect

Four of the five are the same problem at different scales. Parking lot claims a spot in one process with a compare-and-swap. BookMyShow claims a seat across a cluster with a Redis Lua script. Flash sale does the same claim under two million concurrent users. Read them in that order and the primitive stays constant while only the blast radius changes.

Elevator is the outlier: it is the only one with an autonomous control loop, which means it is the only one where the system acts without a user request. That is what makes it the hardest of the machine-coding problems, and why its tick loop and thread model get more space than its class diagram.

Suggested order

If you are preparing a loop rather than browsing: parking lot first, because it is the cheapest place to rehearse naming the axis of change out loud. Then elevator, because the state machine is the piece most people fumble. Then BookMyShow, then flash sale, as a pair — the second is the first one scaled, and reading them together is worth more than either alone. URL shortener last; it is the easiest to pass and the hardest to stand out in, so treat it as a polish exercise.

Field Value

Category Object Design / Machine Coding (LLD-primary, with a scale-up HLD appendix)

Staleness Risk Low (pure OO design; nothing vendor-dependent)
Round type 45–60 min machine coding. You are scored on extensibility, not on feature count.

🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is this round actually testing? Whether "add a new vehicle type / pricing rule" is a new class or an edit to a switch.
Where is the only contended resource? The free-spot set per (floor, spot type). Everything else is effectively single-threaded.
How do you prevent two gates assigning the same spot? Atomic claim — ConcurrentHashMap.compute or a per-floor lock — never check-then-act.
Which two Strategies must exist before the follow-up? SpotAllocationStrategy and PricingStrategy. These are the knobs every follow-up turns.
Money type? BigDecimal or long minor units. double loses the round in one glance.
How many patterns should appear? Three or four. Six is a negative signal — pattern-itis.
What do you cut in scope, out loud? Payments gateway, auth, persistence, reservations, number-plate OCR. Say the cuts.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Cover the labels and redraw from memory. Answer key in §4.

1. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

Spend 4–5 minutes here. Candidates fail this round on scope, not on code.

  1. Multiple floors, or one? Drives whether ParkingLot → Floor → Spot or a flat spot list. Assume multi-floor; it costs nothing and shows foresight.

  2. Which vehicle types, and can a small vehicle take a large spot? This is the real question — the fallback rule is where the allocation strategy earns its existence.

  3. Pricing model? Flat hourly, slab-based (first 2h free, then ₹30/h), per-vehicle-type, day/night differential? Assume it will change — that's the follow-up.

  4. How many entry/exit gates? More than one means concurrency is in scope. If they say one, ask "would you like me to make it thread-safe anyway?" — they will say yes.

  5. Reservations / pre-booking? Usually out of scope. Confirm and cut it explicitly.

  6. Do we track the vehicle, or just the ticket? Affects whether Vehicle is an entity with identity or a value object.

  7. Persistence? In-memory. State it: "repository interfaces backed by ConcurrentHashMap; swapping in JPA is an implementation detail, not a design one."

Scope cuts to announce out loud: payment gateway integration, authentication, number-plate recognition, physical hardware/sensors, multi-lot federation. Naming what you exclude is scored.

2. Functional Requirements

  • Park a vehicle: issue a ticket recording spot, vehicle, entry time.

  • Unpark: compute fee from the ticket, free the spot, close the ticket.

  • Support multiple vehicle types (motorcycle, car, bus/truck) mapped to spot types (small, medium, large).

  • Support a fallback rule: a smaller vehicle may occupy a larger spot when its own type is full (configurable — this is a policy, not a hard-coded if).

  • Query availability per floor and per spot type.

  • Multiple entry and exit gates operating concurrently.

Explicitly out of scope: payments, reservations, auth, valet, EV-charging spots (though see §7 — EV is the classic extensibility follow-up).

3. Non-Functional Requirements

  • Extensibility is requirement #1. Adding a vehicle type, a spot type, an allocation policy, or a pricing rule must be a new class plus a registry entry — never an edit to an existing method. This is the scoring rubric.

  • Thread safety at the spot-assignment boundary. Two gates must never receive the same spot.

  • Testability — constructor injection, Clock injected rather than System.currentTimeMillis(), no static singletons.

  • Correctness of money — BigDecimal or long minor units, never double.

  • Scale for the interview: single lot, ~10k spots, ~10 gates. In-memory is correct. (Real-world scale-up in §9.)

4. Class Model

Answer key for the Visual Recall diagram: A = Vehicle arrives at gate, B = EntryGate, C = spot available?, D = SpotAllocationStrategy, E = Lot full — reject, F = Ticket issued, G = Ticket repository, H = Vehicle at exit, I = ExitGate, J = PricingStrategy, K = Fee charged, spot freed.

The design in one sentence: ParkingLot is a thin facade that owns invariants; all variation lives behind three injected policy interfaces; everything else is data.

5. Core Code — Interfaces and the Skeleton

Value objects and enums

public enum VehicleType { MOTORCYCLE, CAR, BUS }

public enum SpotType {
    SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE;

    /** Larger ordinal fits more. Used by the fit policy, not by business code. */
    public boolean isAtLeast(SpotType other) {
        return this.ordinal() >= other.ordinal();
    }
}

/** Value object — identity is the plate, no lifecycle. */
public record Vehicle(String licensePlate, VehicleType type) {
    public Vehicle {
        Objects.requireNonNull(licensePlate);
        Objects.requireNonNull(type);
    }
}

public record SpotId(int floor, String code) {}
Trap

⚠️ Enum with behaviour (isAtLeast) is high signal for tiny effort. What you must not do is put a switch (vehicleType) inside a pricing or allocation method — that is the exact edit the round is testing for.

The three extension points

These are the knobs every follow-up question turns. Define them before you write ParkingLot.

/** Which spot type(s) may a vehicle occupy, in preference order? */
public interface SpotTypeFitPolicy {
    List<SpotType> acceptableSpotsFor(VehicleType type);
}

/** Given a vehicle, pick and atomically claim a spot. Empty if lot is full. */
public interface SpotAllocationStrategy {
    Optional<ParkingSpot> allocate(Vehicle vehicle, ParkingLot lot);
}

/** Fee for a completed stay. */
public interface PricingStrategy {
    BigDecimal price(Ticket ticket, Instant exitTime);
}

Why three and not one: they vary independently. The customer can change pricing without changing allocation; a new EV spot type changes fit without changing either. One interface doing all three would force an edit for any of the three changes — that is the SRP violation the interviewer is hunting for.

The spot — owns its own invariant

public final class ParkingSpot {
    private final SpotId id;
    private final SpotType type;
    private final AtomicReference<Vehicle> occupant = new AtomicReference<>();

    public ParkingSpot(SpotId id, SpotType type) {
        this.id = id;
        this.type = type;
    }

    public SpotId id()      { return id; }
    public SpotType type()  { return type; }
    public boolean isFree() { return occupant.get() == null; }

    /** Atomic claim. Returns false if another gate won the race. */
    public boolean tryOccupy(Vehicle v) {
        return occupant.compareAndSet(null, v);
    }

    public void release() {
        occupant.set(null);
    }
}
Core point

🔴 This is the concurrency answer. compareAndSet makes the claim atomic without any lock. There is deliberately no public setter for occupant — the state machine is enforced by the class, not by whoever calls it. That's encapsulation of invariants, and interviewers name it.

Allocation — nearest-first, with the fit policy injected

public final class NearestFirstAllocationStrategy implements SpotAllocationStrategy {

    private final SpotTypeFitPolicy fitPolicy;

    public NearestFirstAllocationStrategy(SpotTypeFitPolicy fitPolicy) {
        this.fitPolicy = fitPolicy;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<ParkingSpot> allocate(Vehicle vehicle, ParkingLot lot) {
        // Preference order: exact fit first, then larger spots as fallback.
        for (SpotType candidate : fitPolicy.acceptableSpotsFor(vehicle.type())) {
            for (ParkingFloor floor : lot.floorsNearestFirst()) {
                Optional<ParkingSpot> claimed = floor.claimFreeSpot(candidate, vehicle);
                if (claimed.isPresent()) return claimed;
            }
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }
}

The contended resource — free-spot sets per floor

public final class ParkingFloor {
    private final int level;
    // The ONLY contended structure in the design.
    private final Map<SpotType, Deque<ParkingSpot>> freeByType = new EnumMap<>(SpotType.class);
    private final Map<SpotId, ParkingSpot> allSpots = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public ParkingFloor(int level, List<ParkingSpot> spots) {
        this.level = level;
        for (SpotType t : SpotType.values()) {
            freeByType.put(t, new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>());
        }
        for (ParkingSpot s : spots) {
            allSpots.put(s.id(), s);
            freeByType.get(s.type()).add(s);
        }
    }

    /**
     * Pop-and-claim. The deque pop is atomic; tryOccupy is the second guard.
     * If we lose the CAS (shouldn't happen, but defends against double-add bugs),
     * we simply try the next spot.
     */
    public Optional<ParkingSpot> claimFreeSpot(SpotType type, Vehicle v) {
        Deque<ParkingSpot> free = freeByType.get(type);
        ParkingSpot spot;
        while ((spot = free.pollFirst()) != null) {
            if (spot.tryOccupy(v)) return Optional.of(spot);
            // lost the race — spot already taken; discard and continue
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    public void release(ParkingSpot spot) {
        spot.release();
        freeByType.get(spot.type()).addLast(spot);
    }

    public int level() { return level; }

    public long availableCount(SpotType type) {
        return freeByType.get(type).size();
    }
}
Concurrency

🧵 Say this out loud: "The contended resource is the free-spot deque per (floor, spot type). I use a lock-free deque plus a CAS on the spot itself, so ten gates never serialize on a global lock. The while loop handles the lost-race case by moving to the next spot rather than failing the request."

Pricing — slab-based, the shape they will ask you to change

public final class SlabPricingStrategy implements PricingStrategy {

    /** Ordered slabs: (upToHoursExclusive, ratePerHour). Last slab is the tail rate. */
    public record Slab(long upToHours, BigDecimal ratePerHour) {}

    private final Map<VehicleType, List<Slab>> slabsByType;

    public SlabPricingStrategy(Map<VehicleType, List<Slab>> slabsByType) {
        this.slabsByType = Map.copyOf(slabsByType);
    }

    @Override
    public BigDecimal price(Ticket ticket, Instant exitTime) {
        long hours = billableHours(ticket.entryTime(), exitTime);
        List<Slab> slabs = slabsByType.get(ticket.vehicle().type());

        BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO;
        long consumed = 0;
        for (Slab slab : slabs) {
            if (consumed >= hours) break;
            long inThisSlab = Math.min(hours, slab.upToHours()) - consumed;
            if (inThisSlab > 0) {
                total = total.add(slab.ratePerHour().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(inThisSlab)));
                consumed += inThisSlab;
            }
        }
        // tail: anything beyond the last slab boundary bills at the last rate
        if (consumed < hours) {
            BigDecimal tailRate = slabs.get(slabs.size() - 1).ratePerHour();
            total = total.add(tailRate.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(hours - consumed)));
        }
        return total.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }

    private long billableHours(Instant in, Instant out) {
        long minutes = Duration.between(in, out).toMinutes();
        return Math.max(1, (long) Math.ceil(minutes / 60.0)); // part-hour rounds up, min 1
    }
}

The facade

public final class ParkingLot {

    private final List<ParkingFloor> floors;
    private final SpotAllocationStrategy allocationStrategy;
    private final PricingStrategy pricingStrategy;
    private final TicketRepository tickets;
    private final Clock clock;                    // injected — makes fees testable

    public ParkingLot(List<ParkingFloor> floors,
                      SpotAllocationStrategy allocationStrategy,
                      PricingStrategy pricingStrategy,
                      TicketRepository tickets,
                      Clock clock) {
        this.floors = List.copyOf(floors);
        this.allocationStrategy = allocationStrategy;
        this.pricingStrategy = pricingStrategy;
        this.tickets = tickets;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public Ticket park(Vehicle vehicle) {
        ParkingSpot spot = allocationStrategy.allocate(vehicle, this)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new LotFullException(vehicle.type()));
        Ticket ticket = Ticket.open(vehicle, spot.id(), clock.instant());
        tickets.save(ticket);
        return ticket;
    }

    public Receipt unpark(String ticketId) {
        Ticket ticket = tickets.findOpen(ticketId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new TicketNotFoundException(ticketId));

        Instant exitTime = clock.instant();
        BigDecimal fee = pricingStrategy.price(ticket, exitTime);

        floorOf(ticket.spotId()).release(spotOf(ticket.spotId()));
        ticket.close(exitTime, fee);
        tickets.save(ticket);

        return new Receipt(ticket.id(), fee, exitTime);
    }

    public List<ParkingFloor> floorsNearestFirst() { return floors; }
}
Trap

⚠️ Note what ParkingLot does not do: it doesn't decide which spot, doesn't decide the price, doesn't know vehicle types. It orchestrates and owns invariants. The moment it branches on VehicleType, it has become a god-facade — see ../04-design-patterns/anti-patterns.md §6.

6. Data Flow — Step by Step

Exit flow, compressed: ticket lookup → PricingStrategy.price(ticket, now) → floor.release(spot) (spot returns to the free deque) → ticket closed with fee → receipt. The release is deliberately after pricing, so a pricing failure doesn't free a spot that was never paid for.

7. Key Design Decisions with Justification

Decision Chosen Rejected alternative Why
Spot selection SpotAllocationStrategy interface switch (vehicleType) inside park() The follow-up is always "now allocate nearest to the exit / nearest to a lift". Strategy makes it a new class.
Fee calculation PricingStrategy interface Method on Vehicle or a PricingService with a switch Pricing changes quarterly and independently of allocation. Separate axis, separate interface.
Fit rules SpotTypeFitPolicy interface Hard-coded if (car && !mediumFree) tryLarge() "Can a bike take a car spot?" is a business policy that differs per lot.
Spot occupancy AtomicReference + CAS on the spot synchronized on the whole lot A global lock serializes all gates. CAS gives lock-free claims.
Free-spot tracking ConcurrentLinkedDeque per (floor, type) Scanning all spots for isFree() O(1) claim vs O(n) scan; and the scan is a check-then-act race.
Time Injected Clock System.currentTimeMillis() Fee logic is untestable otherwise. Interviewers specifically look for this.
Money BigDecimal, scale 2, HALF_UP double double loses the round in one glance.
Persistence TicketRepository interface, in-memory impl Direct JPA / schema discussion Keeps the round on object design. State the seam and move on.
Ticket state Ticket.open() / close() intent methods Public setters on status Encapsulated invariant — you cannot close a closed ticket.

The patterns actually used — and the ones deliberately not

Used (four): Strategy ×3 (allocation, pricing, fit), Facade (ParkingLot), Repository (persistence seam), Value Object (Vehicle, SpotId, Money).

Deliberately not used, and say so if asked:

  • Singleton for ParkingLot — you want one instance, which DI gives you. The GoF Singleton adds global state and kills testability.
  • Factory for spots — spots are created once at construction from config. A factory here is ceremony with no future edit prevented.
  • Observer — nothing needs to react asynchronously in the core scope. Add it only if they ask for a display board.
  • Decorator/Builder — no. Six patterns on a parking lot is a negative signal.
Say this

🎤 The line that scores: "I've used Strategy three times because there are exactly three axes the requirements will change along. I've avoided Singleton and Factory here because I can't name a future edit they'd prevent."

8. Failure Modes & Mitigations

Failure Symptom Mitigation in this design
Two gates claim the same spot Double-parked bay, angry driver compareAndSet on the spot; the loser loops to the next spot
Spot leaked (occupied forever) Availability drifts down over days Release in a finally; plus a reconciler sweeping spots whose ticket is closed but spot still occupied
Spot double-added to free deque Same spot handed to two vehicles The tryOccupy CAS is the second guard — a duplicated deque entry fails to claim
Ticket lost by driver Cannot compute fee Lookup by plate as a secondary index; charge a lost-ticket flat fee (a PricingStrategy decorator)
Clock skew across gates Negative or absurd durations Single injected Clock shared by the lot; clamp billableHours to a minimum of 1
Pricing throws Spot freed but no payment Price before release — ordering in unpark() is deliberate
Exit gate crashes mid-unpark Ticket closed, spot not freed Idempotent unpark: closing an already-closed ticket returns the stored receipt; reconciler frees orphan spots

9. Scale Considerations (the "now make it 500 lots" follow-up)

This is where the LLD round briefly becomes HLD. Keep it to two minutes.

  • One lot, many gates → the current design is correct. In-memory state, CAS claims, no network. Do not distribute what fits in a process.

  • One lot, gates as separate processes → the free-spot set moves to Redis. The claim becomes a Lua script or SPOP on a per-(floor,type) set — the same atomic-claim idea, one level out. Never GET then SET.

  • Many lots → shard by lotId. Lots are independent aggregates with no cross-lot transactions, so this shards perfectly. Each lot's state lives in one Redis shard or one DB partition.

  • Persistence → tickets are an append-mostly table partitioned by month; spot occupancy is derived state that can be rebuilt from open tickets. That rebuild path is what makes the Redis copy a cache rather than a second source of truth.

  • Analytics (occupancy over time, revenue) → CDC the ticket table into a columnar store. Never run GROUP BY over tickets on the operational database.

  • What does not change: the three strategy interfaces. That's the payoff of the LLD — the distributed version swaps ParkingFloor's implementation and leaves the domain untouched.

10. Capacity Back-of-Envelope

Only if asked — this is not the point of the round.

  • 10,000 spots, average dwell 2h → ~5,000 park events/day → ~0.06 events/s average, peak maybe 5/s at an office lot's 9am.

  • This is a tiny workload. Say so. "The concurrency here is about correctness at 10 gates, not throughput — a single process handles this with room to spare." Recognising that a problem is small is a senior signal.

  • Memory: 10k spots × ~100 bytes = ~1MB. Tickets at 200 bytes × 5k/day × 90 days retained = ~90MB. Trivially in-memory.

11. Extensibility Follow-Ups (rehearse these — they are the round)

The interviewer will pick two or three. Each should be answerable in under 60 seconds with "new class, no edits."

Follow-up Your answer
"Add EV charging spots" New SpotType.EV_CHARGING; SpotTypeFitPolicy returns it only for EV-capable vehicles; a ChargingSurchargeDecorator wraps PricingStrategy. No edit to ParkingLot.
"First 30 minutes free" New PricingStrategy implementation, or a decorator over the existing one. Registry entry changes; nothing else.
"Allocate nearest to the elevator" New SpotAllocationStrategy; spots gain a distanceToExit field. ParkingLot untouched.
"Support handicapped spots" New SpotType + a fit policy that returns it only for permitted vehicles — the fit policy is precisely the right home for an eligibility rule.
"Monthly pass holders" PricingStrategy returning zero for pass holders, resolved by a PassRepository. Or a PricingStrategy decorator — mention both and pick.
"Show a live availability board" Observer — ParkingFloor publishes SpotOccupied/SpotFreed; the display subscribes. Note the sync-vs-async and listener-exception decisions explicitly.
"Two gates, same spot — prove it can't happen" Walk the CAS. compareAndSet(null, vehicle) — exactly one thread observes null; the other loops to the next spot.
"Now make the whole thing distributed" §9. Redis set per (floor, type), atomic pop, lot as the shard key.
"Reduce it — one floor, one vehicle type" Say you'd delete two of the three strategies. Willingness to remove abstraction is as strong a signal as adding it.

12. 30-Second Verbal Summary + Follow-up Prep

One-paragraph spoken opener

"I'll model this as a ParkingLot facade over floors and spots, with three injected policy interfaces — allocation, pricing, and spot-type fit — because those are the three axes the requirements will change along. Spots own their own occupancy and are claimed with a compare-and-swap, so multiple gates never need a global lock. Money is BigDecimal, time comes from an injected Clock so fees are testable, and persistence sits behind a repository interface backed by a concurrent map. I'm explicitly cutting payments, auth, and reservations. The design goal is that 'add EV spots' or 'first 30 minutes free' is a new class and a registry entry, never an edit to an existing method."

Follow-up questions to prepare for

Tier 1 — Verifier ("did you actually think?")

  • Why BigDecimal and not double?
  • Why is Clock a constructor parameter?
  • Why does ParkingSpot have no public setter?
  • What's your contended resource?

Tier 2 — Mechanism

  • Walk me through two gates racing for the last spot.
  • Why a deque of free spots rather than scanning?
  • Why three strategy interfaces rather than one ParkingPolicy?
  • Where exactly would persistence plug in?

Tier 3 — Failure modes

  • A gate crashes after claiming a spot but before saving the ticket. What happens?
  • How do you detect a leaked spot?
  • Driver loses the ticket — now what?
  • Pricing strategy throws — is the spot freed?

Tier 4 — Open-ended

  • Now 500 lots across a city, one mobile app. What changes?
  • Add reservations — a spot held for a future window. (This is meaningfully harder: it turns the free-set into an interval-availability problem. Say that.)
  • How would you A/B test two pricing strategies?

  • Event-sourced lot — occupancy derived from a SpotOccupied/SpotFreed log. Overkill for this round; mention only if asked about audit.

  • Interval-tree availability — required if reservations enter scope; the free-set model doesn't extend to future time windows.

🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two request types, and why the distinction matters External (hall call: floor + direction) vs internal (car call: floor only). External requests are dispatchable to any car; internal are bound to one.
Why is a single sorted queue wrong? It ignores direction. You need two sets per car — up targets and down targets — serviced in SCAN order.
The core scheduling algorithm? SCAN / LOOK: keep going in the current direction while targets remain ahead; then reverse. Same as disk-head scheduling.
Where does the State pattern go? The car: IDLE / MOVING_UP / MOVING_DOWN / DOORS_OPEN / MAINTENANCE. Each state decides its own legal transitions.
Where does Strategy go? The dispatcher — which car answers a hall call. This is the knob every follow-up turns.
What makes this harder than parking lot? It has an autonomous tick loop. The system acts without a user request, so you must design the loop and its thread model.
Cost function for dispatch, in one line Prefer a car already moving toward the call in the same direction; penalise direction reversal and current load.

🖼️ Visual Recall

1. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

  1. How many cars and how many floors? N cars changes the problem from "scheduling" to "dispatch + scheduling". Assume N cars — a single car is a degenerate case you get for free.

  2. Hall call buttons: up/down separately, or one button per floor? Real buildings have both up and down. This matters — it's what lets you avoid picking up a down-traveller with an up-going car.

  3. Do we simulate physical movement, or is it instantaneous? Ask for a tick-based simulation: one tick = one floor of travel. This makes the whole thing testable and deterministic.

  4. Capacity limits? Weight/passenger count — usually out of scope, but say you'd model it as a LoadPolicy so it's a one-class addition.

  5. Special modes? Maintenance, fire-service, express/VIP. Cut them, but mention MAINTENANCE as a state so the model can hold them.

  6. What's the optimisation target? Average wait time, worst-case wait, or throughput? These give different dispatch algorithms. Asking this is a strong senior signal — most candidates never do.

Scope cuts to announce: physical hardware/sensors, door-obstruction detection, emergency protocols, energy optimisation, real-time OS constraints.

2. Functional Requirements

  • External (hall) request: a user on floor f presses UP or DOWN. The system picks a car.

  • Internal (car) request: a user inside car c presses floor f. Bound to that car.

  • Cars move floor-by-floor, stopping where a target exists, opening and closing doors.

  • A car reverses direction only when no targets remain ahead in the current direction.

  • Query state of any car: current floor, direction, door state, pending targets.

  • Support N cars; dispatch policy is pluggable.

Out of scope: payments (none), auth, persistence (in-memory), physical safety interlocks.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

  • Extensibility: swapping the dispatch algorithm (nearest-car → look-ahead cost → zoned) must be a new class. This is the scoring rubric.

  • Correct state machine: illegal transitions must be impossible, not merely unlikely. A car cannot move with doors open.

  • Thread safety: request submission (many threads: buttons) vs the control loop (one thread per car, or one scheduler). This is the concurrency question you will get.

  • Determinism for tests: tick-driven, with an injected Clock/tick source. A test must be able to assert "after 7 ticks, car 2 is at floor 5, doors open."

  • Interview scale: ≤10 cars, ≤100 floors. Trivial computationally — say so.

4. The State Machine (this is the centrepiece)

Answer key for the Visual Recall: A = IDLE, B = MOVING_UP, C = target above, D = MOVING_DOWN, E = target below, F = DOORS_OPEN, G = arrived at target floor, H = DOORS_CLOSING, I = dwell timer expired, J = no targets remain, K = MAINTENANCE, L = maintenance engaged, M = maintenance cleared.

The two invariants that matter, and that you should state explicitly:

  1. The car never moves with doors open. MOVING_* is reachable only from DOORS_CLOSING or IDLE. This is not a comment — it's enforced by which transitions exist.

  2. Direction only reverses through DOORS_CLOSING or IDLE. There is no MOVING_UP → MOVING_DOWN edge. A car physically cannot flip direction mid-shaft.

Say this

🎤 Say this out loud: "The absence of a MOVING_UP → MOVING_DOWN edge is the design. Reversal has to pass through a stop, which is both physically true and the reason the SCAN algorithm falls out naturally."

5. Component Model

6. Core Code

Enums and requests

public enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

public enum DoorState { OPEN, CLOSING, CLOSED }

public enum CarStatus { IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOORS_OPEN, DOORS_CLOSING, MAINTENANCE }

/** Pressed outside the car: "I am on floor f and I want to go UP." */
public record HallCall(int floor, Direction direction, Instant requestedAt) {}

/** Pressed inside car c: "take me to floor f." */
public record CarCall(int carId, int floor) {}
Trap

⚠️ The distinction candidates miss: a HallCall carries a direction; a CarCall does not. That single field is what lets you avoid stopping an up-going car for a passenger who wants to go down.

The target set — direction-aware, this is the real data structure

/**
 * Targets split by the direction the car will be travelling when it serves them.
 * NavigableSet gives us "next target above / below current floor" in O(log n).
 */
public final class TargetSet {
    private final NavigableSet<Integer> upTargets   = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();
    private final NavigableSet<Integer> downTargets = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();

    public void addUp(int floor)   { upTargets.add(floor); }
    public void addDown(int floor) { downTargets.add(floor); }

    /** Car call: served in whichever direction reaches it. */
    public void add(int floor, int currentFloor) {
        if (floor >= currentFloor) upTargets.add(floor);
        else downTargets.add(floor);
    }

    public boolean hasTargetAbove(int floor) {
        return upTargets.ceiling(floor) != null || downTargets.ceiling(floor) != null;
    }

    public boolean hasTargetBelow(int floor) {
        return upTargets.floor(floor) != null || downTargets.floor(floor) != null;
    }

    /** Should the car stop here, given where it's heading? */
    public boolean shouldStopAt(int floor, Direction heading) {
        return switch (heading) {
            case UP   -> upTargets.contains(floor)
                         || (!hasTargetAbove(floor + 1) && downTargets.contains(floor));
            case DOWN -> downTargets.contains(floor)
                         || (!hasTargetBelow(floor - 1) && upTargets.contains(floor));
            case IDLE -> upTargets.contains(floor) || downTargets.contains(floor);
        };
    }

    public void clearFloor(int floor) {
        upTargets.remove(floor);
        downTargets.remove(floor);
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() { return upTargets.isEmpty() && downTargets.isEmpty(); }

    public int size() { return upTargets.size() + downTargets.size(); }
}
Core point

🔴 The shouldStopAt logic is the SCAN algorithm. Going UP, stop for up-targets. Also stop for a down-target only if nothing remains above — that's the turnaround floor. Getting this right is the difference between a working elevator and one that strands people.

The car — state machine plus one tick

public final class ElevatorCar {

    private final int id;
    private final int minFloor, maxFloor;
    private final TargetSet targets = new TargetSet();
    private final List<CarListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    private volatile int currentFloor;
    private volatile CarStatus status = CarStatus.IDLE;
    private volatile Direction heading = Direction.IDLE;
    private int doorTicksRemaining = 0;

    private static final int DOOR_DWELL_TICKS = 3;

    public ElevatorCar(int id, int minFloor, int maxFloor, int startFloor) {
        this.id = id;
        this.minFloor = minFloor;
        this.maxFloor = maxFloor;
        this.currentFloor = startFloor;
    }

    /** Called from button threads. Synchronised only on the target set mutation. */
    public synchronized void acceptHallCall(HallCall call) {
        if (call.direction() == Direction.UP) targets.addUp(call.floor());
        else targets.addDown(call.floor());
        wakeIfIdle();
    }

    public synchronized void acceptCarCall(int floor) {
        if (floor < minFloor || floor > maxFloor) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("floor out of range: " + floor);
        }
        targets.add(floor, currentFloor);
        wakeIfIdle();
    }

    private void wakeIfIdle() {
        if (status == CarStatus.IDLE && !targets.isEmpty()) {
            if (targets.shouldStopAt(currentFloor, Direction.IDLE)) {
                openDoors();
            } else {
                heading = targets.hasTargetAbove(currentFloor) ? Direction.UP : Direction.DOWN;
                status = (heading == Direction.UP) ? CarStatus.MOVING_UP : CarStatus.MOVING_DOWN;
            }
        }
    }

    /** One simulation tick. Called by the control loop, single-threaded per car. */
    public synchronized void tick() {
        switch (status) {
            case IDLE          -> wakeIfIdle();
            case MOVING_UP     -> step(+1);
            case MOVING_DOWN   -> step(-1);
            case DOORS_OPEN    -> tickDoors();
            case DOORS_CLOSING -> departOrIdle();
            case MAINTENANCE   -> { /* frozen until cleared */ }
        }
    }

    private void step(int delta) {
        currentFloor += delta;
        notifyListeners();
        if (targets.shouldStopAt(currentFloor, heading)) {
            openDoors();
        } else if (!continuesInHeading()) {
            // nothing left ahead — stop and let departOrIdle pick a new heading
            status = CarStatus.DOORS_CLOSING;
        }
    }

    private boolean continuesInHeading() {
        return heading == Direction.UP
                ? targets.hasTargetAbove(currentFloor + 1)
                : targets.hasTargetBelow(currentFloor - 1);
    }

    private void openDoors() {
        targets.clearFloor(currentFloor);
        status = CarStatus.DOORS_OPEN;
        doorTicksRemaining = DOOR_DWELL_TICKS;
        notifyListeners();
    }

    private void tickDoors() {
        if (--doorTicksRemaining <= 0) status = CarStatus.DOORS_CLOSING;
    }

    /** The only place a new heading is chosen. Enforces "no reversal while moving". */
    private void departOrIdle() {
        if (targets.isEmpty()) {
            status = CarStatus.IDLE;
            heading = Direction.IDLE;
        } else if (heading != Direction.DOWN && targets.hasTargetAbove(currentFloor)) {
            heading = Direction.UP;
            status = CarStatus.MOVING_UP;
        } else if (targets.hasTargetBelow(currentFloor)) {
            heading = Direction.DOWN;
            status = CarStatus.MOVING_DOWN;
        } else {
            heading = Direction.UP;                 // reverse
            status = CarStatus.MOVING_UP;
        }
        notifyListeners();
    }

    private void notifyListeners() {
        CarSnapshot snap = snapshot();
        for (CarListener l : listeners) {
            try { l.onCarChanged(snap); }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { /* isolate listener failures */ }
        }
    }

    public void addListener(CarListener l) { listeners.add(l); }

    public CarSnapshot snapshot() {
        return new CarSnapshot(id, currentFloor, status, heading, targets.size());
    }

    public int id()             { return id; }
    public int currentFloor()   { return currentFloor; }
    public Direction heading()  { return heading; }
    public CarStatus status()   { return status; }
    public int pendingCount()   { return targets.size(); }
}

public record CarSnapshot(int id, int floor, CarStatus status, Direction heading, int pending) {}

public interface CarListener { void onCarChanged(CarSnapshot snapshot); }
Concurrency

🧵 The thread model, stated explicitly: button presses call acceptHallCall/acceptCarCall from arbitrary threads; the control loop calls tick() from one thread. Both are synchronized on the car, so a car is a monitor — its state is only ever mutated under its own lock. Cars are independent, so N cars give N-way parallelism with no shared lock. That's the whole concurrency story, and it's short because the boundary was drawn well.

Dispatch — the extension point

public interface DispatchStrategy {
    Optional<ElevatorCar> selectCar(HallCall call, List<ElevatorCar> cars);
}

/** Cost-based LOOK dispatch. The default answer. */
public final class LookAheadDispatchStrategy implements DispatchStrategy {

    private static final int REVERSAL_PENALTY = 1000;
    private static final int LOAD_WEIGHT      = 2;

    @Override
    public Optional<ElevatorCar> selectCar(HallCall call, List<ElevatorCar> cars) {
        return cars.stream()
                .filter(c -> c.status() != CarStatus.MAINTENANCE)
                .min(Comparator.comparingInt(c -> cost(c, call)));
    }

    private int cost(ElevatorCar car, HallCall call) {
        int distance = Math.abs(car.currentFloor() - call.floor());
        int base = distance + LOAD_WEIGHT * car.pendingCount();

        // Ideal: car is already heading toward the call, in the same direction.
        boolean movingToward =
                (car.heading() == Direction.UP   && call.floor() >= car.currentFloor()) ||
                (car.heading() == Direction.DOWN && call.floor() <= car.currentFloor());
        boolean sameDirection = car.heading() == call.direction();

        if (car.status() == CarStatus.IDLE)          return base;
        if (movingToward && sameDirection)           return base;
        return base + REVERSAL_PENALTY;              // car must finish its run and come back
    }
}

Alternative strategies to name (each is a new class, zero edits):

  • NearestCarDispatchStrategy — naive, minimises distance only. Good baseline; visibly worse under load. Mention that it starves cars at building extremities.
  • ZonedDispatchStrategy — each car owns a floor band. Used in tall buildings; trades average wait for predictability.
  • RoundRobinDispatchStrategy — for testing and as a fairness baseline.

The control loop

public final class ElevatorSystem {

    private final List<ElevatorCar> cars;
    private final DispatchStrategy dispatchStrategy;
    private final ScheduledExecutorService ticker;

    public ElevatorSystem(List<ElevatorCar> cars,
                          DispatchStrategy dispatchStrategy,
                          ScheduledExecutorService ticker) {
        this.cars = List.copyOf(cars);
        this.dispatchStrategy = dispatchStrategy;
        this.ticker = ticker;
    }

    public void start(Duration tickInterval) {
        for (ElevatorCar car : cars) {
            // One task per car: cars are independent, so no shared lock.
            ticker.scheduleAtFixedRate(
                    () -> safeTick(car), 0, tickInterval.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        }
    }

    private void safeTick(ElevatorCar car) {
        try {
            car.tick();
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            // A thrown exception silently cancels a scheduled task — never let it escape.
        }
    }

    public void requestFromFloor(HallCall call) {
        dispatchStrategy.selectCar(call, cars)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new NoCarAvailableException(call))
                .acceptHallCall(call);
    }

    public void requestFromInsideCar(CarCall call) {
        carById(call.carId()).acceptCarCall(call.floor());
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        ticker.shutdown();
    }

    private ElevatorCar carById(int id) {
        return cars.stream().filter(c -> c.id() == id).findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("no car " + id));
    }
}
Trap

⚠️ The safeTick wrapper is not defensive padding. scheduleAtFixedRate silently cancels the task if the runnable throws. An uncaught exception in tick() freezes that elevator forever with no error anywhere. This is a genuine production trap and a strong thing to volunteer.

7. Data Flow — a hall call end to end

8. Key Design Decisions with Justification

Decision Chosen Rejected alternative Why
Request modelling HallCall carries direction, CarCall doesn't One Request(floor) type Without direction you stop an up-going car for a down-going passenger. This is the whole point of hall buttons.
Target storage Two NavigableSets (up/down) One PriorityQueue by distance A distance queue makes the car oscillate. SCAN needs direction-partitioned targets.
Scheduling SCAN/LOOK via shouldStopAt FCFS FCFS is O(worst) wait and visibly wrong when demonstrated. Name it as the rejected baseline.
Dispatch DispatchStrategy interface if chain inside ElevatorSystem Every follow-up is "now optimise for X". Strategy makes it a new class.
Car state Explicit CarStatus enum + guarded transitions Boolean flags (isMoving, doorsOpen) Flags permit illegal combinations (moving + doors open). The enum makes them unrepresentable.
Direction reversal Only via DOORS_CLOSING/IDLE Direct MOVING_UP → MOVING_DOWN Physically impossible, and the constraint is what produces correct SCAN behaviour.
Concurrency Car as a monitor (synchronized methods) One global lock over the system Cars are independent aggregates. Per-car locking gives N-way parallelism.
Time Tick-driven via injected ScheduledExecutorService Thread.sleep in a while(true) Tests can drive ticks manually and assert exact positions.
Listener failures Caught per listener Let them propagate One broken floor display must not freeze an elevator.

Patterns used — and the count

Used (four): State (car status machine), Strategy (dispatch), Observer (displays/metrics), Facade (ElevatorSystem).

Considered and rejected: Command for requests — a HallCall record is sufficient; Command earns its place only if you need undo/replay/queueing of requests as objects, which nothing here asks for. Say this if pushed. (→ ../04-design-patterns/anti-patterns.md §1)

9. Failure Modes & Mitigations

Failure Symptom Mitigation
Exception escapes tick() One car freezes permanently, no error logged safeTick try/catch — scheduleAtFixedRate silently cancels on throw
Starvation at building extremities Top-floor callers wait minutes under load Age the request: add a wait-time term to the cost function, or reserve a car above a wait threshold
Car oscillation Car ping-pongs between two floors Direction-partitioned targets + reversal only at the ends. This is what SCAN prevents
Lost hall call Nobody comes Hall calls are held by the system until a car acknowledges; if the assigned car enters MAINTENANCE, re-dispatch its unstarted hall calls
All cars in MAINTENANCE NoCarAvailableException Explicit exception rather than a silent no-op; surface it on the hall display
Doors held open indefinitely Car unavailable Dwell counter with a max-hold cap; after N ticks force DOORS_CLOSING and alarm
Clock/tick drift Simulation diverges from wall time Tick count is the source of truth, not wall time. Assert on ticks in tests
Listener slow (blocking display) Tick loop stalls, all cars lag Dispatch listener notifications asynchronously, or bound them with a timeout

10. Scale Considerations (the "make it a building fleet" follow-up)

Two minutes, no more.

  • One building, ≤16 cars → the current design is right. In-process, one monitor per car. Do not distribute this.

  • Multiple buildings / a campus → each building is an independent aggregate. Shard by buildingId; there are no cross-building transactions, so it shards perfectly.

  • Destination dispatch (the modern real-world design) → users enter their destination at the lobby panel rather than pressing up/down. The system then knows the full origin→destination pair before assigning a car, and can group passengers going to the same floors. This changes the dispatch strategy and nothing else — which is the payoff of having it behind an interface. Worth naming; it signals you know the domain beyond the textbook problem.

  • Predictive positioning → park idle cars at historically high-demand floors by time of day. A new IdlePositioningPolicy; the car and state machine are untouched.

  • Persistence → none needed for control. Emit CarSnapshot events to a metrics store for wait-time SLOs; that's an Observer, already in the design.

11. Testing Strategy (bring this up unprompted — it's rare and scores)

Tick-determinism is what makes this design testable, so demonstrate it:

@Test
void carStopsForUpCallOnTheWayAndDefersDownCall() {
    ElevatorCar car = new ElevatorCar(1, 0, 10, 0);
    car.acceptCarCall(8);              // heading UP toward 8
    car.acceptHallCall(new HallCall(3, Direction.UP, Instant.EPOCH));
    car.acceptHallCall(new HallCall(5, Direction.DOWN, Instant.EPOCH));

    tick(car, 3);                       // 0 -> 3
    assertEquals(3, car.currentFloor());
    assertEquals(CarStatus.DOORS_OPEN, car.status());   // stopped: up-call at 3

    tick(car, 4);                       // dwell 3 + close, then move
    tick(car, 2);                       // 3 -> 5
    assertEquals(5, car.currentFloor());
    assertEquals(CarStatus.MOVING_UP, car.status());    // did NOT stop: 5 is a DOWN call
}

private static void tick(ElevatorCar car, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) car.tick();
}

Test cases to name even if you don't write them: single car single call; up-call served on the way; down-call correctly skipped while heading up; turnaround at the topmost target; idle car on the requested floor opens immediately without moving; maintenance mid-run; two cars racing for one hall call (dispatch determinism).

12. 30-Second Verbal Summary + Follow-up Prep

One-paragraph spoken opener

"I'll separate three things: the car's state machine, the per-car scheduling, and the fleet dispatch. Each car is a monitor holding two direction-partitioned target sets, and it runs the SCAN algorithm — keep going while targets remain ahead, reverse only at the ends. Its status is an explicit enum, so 'moving with doors open' is unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely. Which car answers a hall call is a DispatchStrategy — a cost function over distance, load, and direction-reversal penalty — because that's the axis every follow-up changes. The whole thing is tick-driven from a scheduled executor, one task per car, which gives N-way parallelism with no shared lock and makes the behaviour deterministic in tests. I'm cutting hardware, safety interlocks, and capacity limits."

Follow-up questions to prepare for

Tier 1 — Verifier

  • Why does a hall call carry a direction but a car call doesn't?
  • Why two target sets instead of one sorted queue?
  • What stops the car from moving with the doors open?
  • What's the thread model?

Tier 2 — Mechanism

  • Walk me through the car deciding whether to stop at floor 5.
  • How does the turnaround work — where exactly does direction flip?
  • Trace two cars competing for one hall call.
  • Why one scheduled task per car rather than one loop over all cars?

Tier 3 — Failure modes

  • tick() throws. What happens? (→ the scheduleAtFixedRate cancellation trap)
  • A car goes into maintenance holding three unserved hall calls. Now what?
  • Someone on floor 40 has been waiting four minutes. Why, and how do you fix it?
  • A floor display is slow. Does it slow the elevator?

Tier 4 — Open-ended

  • Optimise for worst-case wait rather than average. What changes? (Answer: the cost function gains an aging term; possibly reserve a car past a threshold.)
  • Implement destination dispatch.
  • 100 floors, 20 cars, morning rush — all requests are lobby→up. What's your strategy? (Zoning + parking idle cars at the lobby.)
  • How would you A/B test two dispatch strategies in a live building?

  • Event-driven instead of tick-driven — cars emit "arrived at floor" events rather than being polled. Closer to real hardware; harder to test deterministically. Name the trade.

  • Global optimiser — recompute the assignment of all pending calls to all cars on every event (an assignment problem). Optimal, expensive, and it makes assignments unstable — a call can be reassigned repeatedly. Real systems use sticky heuristics for this reason.

🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one question this round is really asking How do two users clicking the same seat at the same millisecond not both get it?
Why can't you just lock the seat row and hold it through payment? Payment takes 30–300s. A DB lock held that long destroys throughput and dies with the connection.
The correct primitive Hold-then-confirm — a short-TTL reservation (~8 min) claimed atomically, then converted to a booking on payment success.
Atomic claim mechanism Redis Lua script over a per-show seat hash, or UPDATE ... WHERE status='FREE' and check rowsAffected. Never check-then-act.
Two expiry mechanisms, and which to use Lazy expiry-on-read (correctness) + a sweeper (hygiene). Use both; lazy alone leaves stale rows, sweeper alone has a race window.
What stops a payment retry double-booking? Idempotency key stored in the same transaction as the booking write.
Why is the seat map cached but the hold is not? Seat availability display tolerates 1–2s staleness. The claim must be linearizable. Different consistency per operation.
What's the shard key? showId. All seat contention is within one show; there are no cross-show transactions.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Cover the labels; redraw from memory. Answer key in §6.

1. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

  1. Assigned seating or general admission? Assigned — that's what makes it interesting. GA is just a counter.

  2. Scale? Ask for numbers. "A few hundred cinemas, ~100k concurrent users at peak, but a blockbuster opening means 50k users on one show." That last number is the design driver — the contention is concentrated, not spread.

  3. How long may a seat be held during payment? Get a number. 8–10 minutes is standard. This single number determines your entire hold design.

  4. Can a user book seats across two screens/shows atomically? Say no, and confirm. If yes, you've been handed a distributed transaction and should say so out loud.

  5. Payments in scope? Model it as an async external call with webhook callback. Don't design a payment gateway.

  6. Seat pricing — uniform or by class? Recliner/premium/regular tiers, plus surge for opening weekend. Assume it varies → PricingStrategy.

  7. Do we need to prevent single-seat gaps? ("Don't leave one empty seat between bookings.") A real BookMyShow rule. Great scope question — model it as a SeatSelectionPolicy and cut it.

Scope cuts to announce: recommendations, reviews, food & beverage ordering, loyalty programs, refunds/cancellation flows (mention that cancellation is a compensating transaction and move on).

2. Functional Requirements

  • Browse: city → movie → cinema → show, with showtimes.

  • View the seat map for a show with live-ish availability.

  • Select and hold N seats for a bounded window (8 min).

  • Pay; on success the hold becomes a confirmed booking. On failure or timeout, seats return to the pool.

  • View booking history; cancel (compensating transaction, out of scope for detail).

  • Admin: create cinemas, screens, seat layouts, shows.

The invariant, stated as the one thing that must never break: a seat in a given show is held or booked by at most one user.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

Requirement Target Why it drives the design
No double-booking Absolute. Zero tolerance. This is a correctness requirement, not an SLO. It forces linearizable claims.
Seat-map read latency P99 < 200ms Reads dominate 100:1. Cache aggressively; accept 1–2s staleness.
Hold latency P99 < 100ms The user is clicking. Must be one atomic op, not a transaction across services.
Availability 99.9% Booking is revenue-critical but not life-critical.
Consistency Per-operation. Browse = eventual. Hold/confirm = strong. Saying this out loud is the senior signal. Do not pick one level for the whole system.
Peak concentration 50k users on one show Hot partition. The design must survive contention on a single showId.

4. Capacity Back-of-Envelope

  • Scale assumption: 1,000 cinemas × 5 screens × 5 shows/day = 25,000 shows/day; ~200 seats per screen → 5M seats/day of inventory.

  • Bookings: at 40% occupancy → 2M booked seats/day ≈ 23 seats/s average. Utterly ordinary.

  • Reads: browse-to-book ratio ~100:1 → ~2,300 reads/s average, peak maybe 20k/s at a blockbuster open. This is a caching problem, not a database problem.

  • The number that matters: a blockbuster opening puts ~50k users on one show's seat map, all hammering ~200 seats. Average throughput is irrelevant; contention on one partition is the design driver. Say this explicitly — it reframes the whole problem and it's what separates a good answer from a generic one.

  • Storage: a booking row ~500 bytes × 2M/day × 365 = ~365GB/year. Partition by month; archive beyond 2 years. Seat inventory is derived state, rebuildable from bookings.

  • Redis working set: only active shows need to be hot. ~25k shows × 200 seats × ~50 bytes ≈ 250MB. Trivially fits in memory — mention this, it justifies Redis as the claim authority.

5. High-Level Architecture

The one architectural claim to defend: the Seat service owns seat state, and Redis is the authority during the show's sale window — not Postgres. Postgres holds the durable booking record. This split is what lets a hold be a single ~1ms atomic op instead of a distributed transaction.

6. The Seat State Machine (the centrepiece)

Answer key for Visual Recall: A = AVAILABLE, B = HELD, C = hold claimed, D = TTL expired or released, E = PAYMENT_PENDING, F = checkout started, G = BOOKED, H = payment success, I = payment failed or timeout.

Trap

⚠️ Why PAYMENT_PENDING is a distinct state, not just a longer HELD. Once the user is at the payment gateway you must not let the TTL silently release the seat — a payment could succeed a second after expiry and you'd have taken money for a seat you resold. Entering PAYMENT_PENDING extends the deadline and hands ownership to the saga. Volunteering this distinction is a strong signal; most candidates model one HELD state and get caught by the follow-up.

7. The Concurrency Answer (this is the round)

Why the obvious approaches fail — name these before giving your answer

Approach Why it fails
SELECT status FROM seats ... then UPDATE Classic check-then-act race. Two threads both read FREE.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE held through payment Payment takes 30–300s. A row lock held that long collapses throughput and dies with the connection.
A global mutex over the booking service Serialises every user in the country. Throughput ≈ 1/latency.
Distributed lock (Redlock) per seat Works, but you've added a lock service and its failure modes to get what a single atomic op already gives you. Also lock-expiry-during-work is a real correctness hole without fencing tokens.
Optimistic version column Works, and is the right answer if Redis is off the table. Higher latency, and under 50k-user contention the retry rate is brutal.

The answer: atomic hold with TTL

Primary — Redis Lua, one round trip, all-or-nothing across N seats:

-- KEYS[1] = "show:{showId}:seats"      (hash: seatId -> "FREE" | holdToken | "BOOKED")
-- KEYS[2] = "show:{showId}:holds"      (hash: seatId -> expiryEpochMillis)
-- ARGV[1] = holdToken (idempotency key, one per user attempt)
-- ARGV[2] = expiryEpochMillis
-- ARGV[3] = nowEpochMillis
-- ARGV[4..] = seatIds
local token, expiry, now = ARGV[1], ARGV[2], tonumber(ARGV[3])

-- Phase 1: verify EVERY seat is claimable. All-or-nothing.
for i = 4, #ARGV do
  local seat  = ARGV[i]
  local state = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], seat)
  if state ~= false and state ~= 'FREE' then
    -- occupied — but is it a stale hold? (lazy expiry)
    local exp = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[2], seat)
    if state == 'BOOKED' or exp == false or tonumber(exp) > now then
      return {0, seat}          -- genuinely taken; report which seat
    end
  end
end

-- Phase 2: claim them all.
for i = 4, #ARGV do
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], ARGV[i], token)
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[2], ARGV[i], expiry)
end
return {1, token}

Why this is correct and cheap:

  • Redis executes a script atomically — no other command interleaves. The check-then-act race is structurally impossible, not merely unlikely.
  • All-or-nothing across N seats — a user asking for 4 adjacent seats gets all four or none. No partial holds to clean up.
  • Lazy expiry is inside the script — a stale hold is reclaimed during the same atomic op, so correctness never depends on the sweeper running.
  • One network round trip, ~1ms. Compare to a distributed transaction.
  • {showId} in the key uses a hash tag so all of a show's keys land on one Redis Cluster slot — required for multi-key scripts.

Fallback — pure SQL, if the interviewer removes Redis:

UPDATE seat_inventory
   SET status = 'HELD', hold_token = :token, hold_expires_at = :expiry
 WHERE show_id = :showId
   AND seat_id = ANY(:seatIds)
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'
        OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now()));
-- then: if rowsAffected <> :expectedCount -> roll back, report conflict
Core point

🔴 The whole trick is rowsAffected. The database does the check and the act in one statement under its own row locks; you never read-then-write. The OR (status='HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now()) clause is the lazy expiry. Row locks are held for microseconds, not for the duration of payment.

Expiry — you need both mechanisms, and should say why

Mechanism Role
Lazy expiry on read/claim Correctness. A stale hold is reclaimed the instant someone tries to claim that seat. Works even if the sweeper is down.
Background sweeper (every 30s) Hygiene. Frees seats nobody is asking for, so the seat map shows them as available and the user sees truth.

Lazy alone → the seat map lies (shows held, actually free). Sweeper alone → a race window between expiry and sweep. Both, and say why each exists.

Idempotency — the payment retry

The user's payment webhook can fire twice. The confirm must be idempotent:

@Transactional
public Booking confirm(String holdToken, String idempotencyKey, PaymentRef payment) {
    // Same transaction as the business write — this is the whole point.
    Optional<Booking> existing = bookings.findByIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey);
    if (existing.isPresent()) return existing.get();     // replay: return stored result

    Hold hold = seatService.validateHold(holdToken)      // still ours? not expired?
            .orElseThrow(() -> new HoldExpiredException(holdToken));

    Booking booking = Booking.confirm(hold, payment, clock.instant());
    bookings.save(booking);                              // includes idempotencyKey column (UNIQUE)
    outbox.save(new BookingConfirmedEvent(booking));     // same txn — no dual write
    return booking;
}
// after commit: seatService.markBooked(holdToken) flips Redis FREE->BOOKED permanently
Trap

⚠️ Two things that must be in the same transaction: the booking row and the idempotency key (or you get a crash window where the booking happened but the key wasn't recorded), and the booking row and the outbox row (or you get a dual-write and lose the event). A UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_key is the backstop that makes a concurrent duplicate fail loudly rather than silently double-book.

8. Data Flow — Step by Step

9. LLD — Class Model

The interviewer may ask for this instead of, or after, the architecture.

public enum SeatStatus { AVAILABLE, HELD, PAYMENT_PENDING, BOOKED }

public record SeatId(String showId, String seatCode) {}

/** Value object. Seat *class* drives pricing; seat *state* lives in the inventory. */
public record Seat(String seatCode, int row, int number, SeatClass seatClass) {}

public enum SeatClass { REGULAR, PREMIUM, RECLINER }

/** The extension points — define these before anything else. */
public interface SeatHoldStore {
    /** All-or-nothing. Empty if any seat is unavailable. */
    Optional<Hold> tryHold(String showId, List<String> seatCodes, String token, Duration ttl);
    Optional<Hold> validate(String token);
    void release(String token);
    void markBooked(String token);
}

public interface PricingStrategy {
    Money priceFor(Show show, List<Seat> seats, Customer customer);
}

public interface SeatSelectionPolicy {
    /** e.g. reject selections that strand a single empty seat. */
    void validate(List<String> requested, SeatMap currentMap) throws InvalidSelectionException;
}

public final class Hold {
    private final String token;
    private final String showId;
    private final List<String> seatCodes;
    private final Instant expiresAt;
    private volatile SeatStatus status;

    // no public setter — transitions are intent methods that enforce legality
    public void enterPaymentPending(Instant newDeadline) {
        if (status != SeatStatus.HELD) {
            throw new IllegalStateTransitionException(status, SeatStatus.PAYMENT_PENDING);
        }
        this.status = SeatStatus.PAYMENT_PENDING;
    }

    public boolean isExpired(Clock clock) { return clock.instant().isAfter(expiresAt); }
}

public final class BookingService {

    private final SeatHoldStore holds;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private final SeatSelectionPolicy selectionPolicy;
    private final BookingRepository bookings;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final Clock clock;

    public HoldResponse hold(HoldRequest req) {
        selectionPolicy.validate(req.seatCodes(), seatMapOf(req.showId()));
        return holds.tryHold(req.showId(), req.seatCodes(), req.idempotencyKey(), Duration.ofMinutes(8))
                .map(h -> new HoldResponse(h.token(), h.expiresAt(),
                                           pricing.priceFor(showOf(req.showId()), seatsOf(req), req.customer())))
                .orElseThrow(() -> new SeatsUnavailableException(req.seatCodes()));
    }
    // confirm(...) as shown in §7
}

Patterns used (four): Strategy (pricing, selection policy), State (hold/seat lifecycle), Repository (persistence seam), Saga/Orchestrator (payment). Not used: Singleton, Builder, Decorator — no future edit they'd prevent here.

10. Key Design Decisions with Justification

Decision Chosen Rejected Why
Seat claim Redis Lua, atomic, all-or-nothing SELECT then UPDATE Check-then-act races. Lua makes interleaving structurally impossible.
Lock duration Short-TTL hold, released by TTL DB lock held through payment Payment is 30–300s. Row locks that long collapse throughput.
Claim authority Redis during the sale window Postgres as authority ~1ms vs ~10ms, and it keeps a hot show's contention off the primary. Postgres remains the durable record.
Expiry Lazy and sweeper Either alone Lazy = correctness, sweeper = the seat map telling the truth.
Payment consistency Saga with compensations 2PC across booking and payment 2PC blocks on coordinator failure and can't span an external PSP anyway.
Event publishing Transactional outbox Write DB then publish to Kafka Dual write loses events on crash between the two.
Retry safety Idempotency key, same txn, UNIQUE constraint Dedupe in the app layer only The constraint is what makes a concurrent duplicate fail loudly.
Consistency model Per-operation: browse eventual, claim strong One level for the whole system Naming this per-operation is the senior signal.
Sharding By showId By userId or cityId All contention is within a show; no cross-show transactions. Shards perfectly.
Seat map reads Cached 1–2s + WebSocket delta push Always live from Redis 100:1 read ratio. A 2s-stale map is fine because the claim is authoritative — the user just sees a 409 occasionally.
Better

✅ The framing that lands: "The seat map is allowed to lie for two seconds. The claim is not allowed to lie ever. Those are different consistency requirements on the same data, and putting them in the same tier is what makes people over-engineer this problem."

11. Failure Modes & Mitigations

Failure Symptom Mitigation
Two users claim the same seat Double-booking — the cardinal sin Atomic Lua / rowsAffected. Structurally impossible, not probabilistically rare.
Redis dies mid-sale Seat state lost Redis AOF everysec + replica; on failover, rebuild from Postgres bookings (BOOKED is durable; holds are safely lost — worst case a user re-picks). State the rebuild path — this is what makes Redis a cache, not a second truth.
User abandons at payment page Seats stuck in PAYMENT_PENDING Saga timeout (15 min) → compensate → release. Never rely on the user.
Payment succeeds after hold expired Money taken, seat resold This is why PAYMENT_PENDING exists — the TTL does not auto-release it. Saga owns the deadline. If it still happens: refund + compensate, and alert.
Payment webhook delivered twice Double booking / double charge Idempotency key in the same transaction, UNIQUE constraint as backstop.
Webhook never arrives Booking stuck pending Reconciler polls the PSP for pending payments older than 5 min. Never trust a webhook as the only path.
Hot show saturates one Redis shard Latency spike on blockbuster open Hash-tag per show keeps it on one slot by design; scale by adding shards (other shows move away) and add a local JVM "sold out" flag to short-circuit.
Sweeper down Seat map shows held seats that are free Lazy expiry keeps correctness; only display is stale. Alert on sweeper lag.
Cache stampede on seat map Redis hammered when a hot show's cache expires Single-flight / request coalescing per showId.
Overselling via admin edit Seat count changed mid-sale Seat layout is immutable once a show opens. Version the layout instead.

12. Scale Considerations

  • Hot partition is the real problem, not aggregate throughput. 23 bookings/s average is nothing; 50k users on one show is everything. Every scaling decision should be justified against the hot-show case.

  • Read scaling: CDN for static seat layout (SVG), Redis cache for the availability overlay, WebSocket push for deltas instead of polling. Polling 50k clients every 2s is 25k req/s of pure waste.

  • Write scaling: shard Redis and Postgres by showId. A show is a natural aggregate boundary — no cross-shard transactions ever.

  • Waiting room / queue for blockbuster on-sales — the flash-sale pattern. Admit N users per second into the booking flow; everyone else sees a position. (→ high-concurrency-flash-sale-system.md)

  • Multi-region: shows are geographically local. Route by city → region; a Mumbai show's data need not leave the Mumbai region. This makes strong consistency cheap because the quorum is in-region.

  • Analytics (occupancy, revenue, popular showtimes) → CDC from Postgres into a columnar warehouse. Never GROUP BY on the booking primary.

13. 30-Second Verbal Summary + Follow-up Prep

One-paragraph spoken opener

"The entire problem is: two users click the same seat in the same millisecond. My answer is hold-then-confirm. A hold is an atomic, all-or-nothing claim on N seats with an 8-minute TTL, executed as a single Redis Lua script — Redis runs scripts atomically, so the check-then-act race is structurally impossible rather than just unlikely. Redis is the claim authority during the sale window; Postgres holds the durable booking and can rebuild Redis after a failure. Payment runs as a saga with compensations, and confirm is idempotent — the idempotency key is written in the same transaction as the booking, with a unique constraint as the backstop. Expiry is both lazy and swept: lazy for correctness, the sweeper so the seat map tells the truth. And I'd note the consistency requirement differs per operation — the seat map may be two seconds stale, the claim may never be wrong."

Follow-up questions to prepare for

Tier 1 — Verifier

  • Why not SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?
  • Why does the hold need a TTL at all?
  • Why is PAYMENT_PENDING separate from HELD?
  • Why BigDecimal/minor units for money?

Tier 2 — Mechanism

  • Walk me through two users claiming seat A1 simultaneously, line by line through the Lua.
  • Why both lazy expiry and a sweeper?
  • How does the idempotency key prevent a double booking on webhook retry?
  • Why hash-tag the Redis key with {showId}?

Tier 3 — Failure modes

  • Redis loses all data mid-sale. What's your recovery?
  • Payment succeeds 1 second after the hold expired. What happens to the money and the seat?
  • The webhook never arrives. How does the booking resolve?
  • The sweeper has been down for an hour. What's broken and what isn't?

Tier 4 — Open-ended

  • Blockbuster on-sale: 500k users at 9:00:00 for one show. Redesign the entry path. (→ waiting room, admission control, static-first)
  • Add "don't leave a single empty seat" as a rule. Where does it go, and what does it cost? (→ SeatSelectionPolicy; it makes the claim non-commutative, so it must be evaluated inside the atomic step or you get races.)
  • Support booking seats across two adjacent screens atomically.
  • How would you price dynamically by demand without breaking the quote the user was shown?

  • Per-show single-writer actor (one thread/partition owns a show's seat map): removes locking entirely by removing concurrency. Elegant; adds a routing and failover problem. Mention if they push on alternatives.

  • Event-sourced seat inventory: audit for free, rebuild by replay, but projection lag becomes user-visible on the seat map. Overkill unless audit is a hard requirement.
