🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Read:write ratio, and what it implies ~100:1. This is a caching and read-path problem; the write path is almost irrelevant.
Why 7 characters of Base62? 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion. Enough for ~100 years at 1B links/year. 6 chars (56B) runs out too soon.
Why NOT hash the long URL (MD5/SHA) and truncate? Truncation collides, and you must then do a read-before-write to detect it — a race and an extra round trip on every create.
The preferred ID scheme Pre-allocated counter ranges (a key-generation service hands each app node a block of 10k), Base62-encoded. No coordination on the hot path.
301 vs 302 — which and why 302 (or 307). A 301 is cached by the browser forever, so you never see the click again — analytics dies and you can't ever change or expire the link.
Where does the redirect actually get served? Redis (or the CDN edge), not the database. P99 target < 50ms.
What's the cache hit rate you'd expect? 90–95%+. Link popularity is extremely Zipfian — a tiny fraction of links take most traffic.
How do you handle a custom alias collision? Unique constraint on the alias column; let the insert fail and return 409. Never check-then-insert.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Cover the labels; redraw from memory. Answer key in §5.

1. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

  1. Scale? Push for numbers. "100M new links/day, 10B redirects/day" is a good working assumption — and it immediately establishes the 100:1 read:write ratio that drives everything.

  2. Custom aliases? Yes changes the ID design materially (you now need a uniqueness check on user-supplied strings alongside generated ones).

  3. Expiry / TTL on links? Yes → you need a deletion story and it rules out permanent 301 caching.

  4. Analytics — what granularity? "Total clicks" is trivial. "Clicks by country, referrer, device, over time" is a whole second system. Ask, then scope it to an async pipeline.

  5. Can the same long URL produce the same short code? If yes, you need a reverse index (long_url → code) and dedup on write. If no (the usual answer), creation is a pure insert — much simpler. Ask this; it's the highest-leverage clarifying question in the problem.

  6. Who can create links — authenticated users only? Drives rate limiting and abuse handling.

  7. Latency target for redirect? Get a number. P99 < 50ms is standard and justifies the cache-first read path.

Scope cuts to announce: link preview/unfurling, QR generation, A/B link splitting, branded domains, malware scanning (mention it as a real requirement you'd put on the write path async, then cut).

2. Functional Requirements

  • Create: POST /api/links {longUrl, customAlias?, expiresAt?} → returns short.ly/aB3xY9z.

  • Redirect: GET /{code} → 302 to the long URL.

  • Custom alias: user-supplied code, reserved if available, 409 if not.

  • Expiry: links may have a TTL; expired links return 410 Gone (semantically better than 404 — it says "this existed").

  • Analytics: click count, and time/geo/referrer breakdown, eventually consistent.

  • Delete / disable a link.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

Requirement Target Consequence for the design
Redirect latency P99 < 50ms globally Cache-first; CDN/edge for the hottest links. The DB is not on the happy path.
Availability (redirect) 99.99% A dead redirect breaks every link ever shared. This is the tier-1 path.
Availability (create) 99.9% Less critical — a failed create is retried by the user.
Durability No lost links, ever A lost mapping breaks links permanently and publicly. Replicated, backed up.
Consistency Read-your-writes on create; eventual for analytics The creator must see their link work immediately. Click counts may lag minutes.
Scale 10B redirects/day, 100M creates/day ~115k redirects/s average, ~350k/s peak.
Short codes Short, URL-safe, non-sequential-looking Base62; sequential counters must be scrambled (§6) or you leak volume and enable enumeration.

4. Capacity Back-of-Envelope

Traffic

  • Creates: 100M/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,160 writes/s average, ~3.5k/s peak.

  • Redirects: 10B/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 115k reads/s average, ~350k/s peak (3× factor).

  • Ratio ≈ 100:1. Say this number out loud early — it justifies every subsequent decision.

Storage

  • Per row: code (7B) + long URL (~500B avg) + user ID (8B) + timestamps (16B) + metadata ≈ ~600 bytes.

  • 100M/day × 600B = 60 GB/day ≈ 22 TB/year. Non-trivial → partitioning and an archive tier from day one.

  • 5-year retention ≈ 110 TB. Comfortable for a partitioned cluster; not for a single node.

Cache

  • Assume the classic 80/20 (actually more like 95/5 for links): cache the hot ~20M links/day → 20M × 600B ≈ 12 GB. Fits in a modest Redis cluster with room to spare. This is the key number — it's what makes a 95% hit rate cheap.

Key space

Length Base62 combinations Runway at 100M/day
6 56.8 billion ~1.5 years
7 3.52 trillion ~96 years ✅
8 218 trillion ~6,000 years (wasteful)

7 characters. Justify it with this table — it's the cleanest "I did the math" moment in the whole problem.

Bandwidth

  • Redirect response is a header-only 302, ~500 bytes. 115k/s × 500B ≈ 58 MB/s ≈ 0.5 Gbps. Trivial. The load is request rate, not bandwidth — worth stating, because it points at connection handling rather than pipes.

5. High-Level Architecture

Answer key for Visual Recall: A = client GET /code, B = redirect service, C = cache hit?, D = 302 redirect, E = database lookup, F = populate cache, G = 404/410, H = async click event, I = analytics store.

Read and write paths are separate services. They have a 100:1 traffic ratio, different availability targets, and different scaling curves. Deploying them together means scaling the write path 100× for no reason and coupling their failure domains. Say this — it's a cheap architectural point most candidates miss.

6. Key Generation (the part that differentiates you)

The four approaches — know all four, recommend one

Approach How Verdict
Hash + truncate (MD5/SHA of long URL, take 7 chars) Deterministic, no coordination ❌ Collides. Truncating destroys uniqueness, so every create needs a read-before-write to check — an extra round trip and a check-then-act race. Reject it explicitly.
Random 7 chars Generate, insert, retry on unique-constraint violation 🟡 Works. Fine at low fill. As the space fills, retry rate climbs. No coordination needed — genuinely fine for most real systems.
Global counter → Base62 One atomic counter, encode 🟡 Correct but the counter is a single hot point, and codes are sequential — enumerable, and they leak your volume.
Pre-allocated counter ranges ✅ A key-gen service hands each app node a block of 10,000 IDs; the node serves them locally ✅ Recommend this. No coordination on the hot path, no collisions by construction, survives KGS downtime for 10k links per node.

The recommended design

/**
 * Each app node leases a block of IDs and serves them from memory.
 * One DB round trip per 10,000 links instead of per link.
 */
public final class RangeBasedKeyGenerator implements KeyGenerator {

    private static final int BLOCK_SIZE = 10_000;
    private static final double REFILL_THRESHOLD = 0.2;   // refill when 20% remains

    private final RangeAllocator allocator;
    private final AtomicLong cursor  = new AtomicLong();
    private volatile long blockEnd   = -1;

    public RangeBasedKeyGenerator(RangeAllocator allocator) {
        this.allocator = allocator;
        leaseNewBlock();
    }

    @Override
    public String nextCode() {
        long id = cursor.getAndIncrement();
        if (id >= blockEnd) {
            synchronized (this) {
                if (id >= blockEnd) leaseNewBlock();      // double-checked, blockEnd is volatile
            }
            id = cursor.getAndIncrement();
        }
        return Base62.encode(scramble(id));
    }

    private void leaseNewBlock() {
        // Atomic in the DB: UPDATE ranges SET next = next + 10000 RETURNING next - 10000
        long start = allocator.allocateBlock(BLOCK_SIZE);
        cursor.set(start);
        blockEnd = start + BLOCK_SIZE;
    }

    /**
     * Sequential ids leak volume and invite enumeration, so the counter is
     * permuted before encoding. This is a 4-round Feistel network over 42 bits
     * — a bijection by construction, so distinct ids can never collide.
     *
     * Cycle-walking keeps the output inside the 7-character space: 62^7 is
     * about 80% of 2^42, so re-applying the permutation until the value fits
     * costs ~1.25 rounds on average and is still a bijection onto [0, 62^7).
     */
    private static final long SPACE = 3_521_614_606_208L;   // 62^7
    private static final int  MASK21 = (1 << 21) - 1;
    private static final int[] ROUND_KEYS =
            { 0x9E3779B1, 0x85EBCA6B, 0xC2B2AE35, 0x27D4EB2F };

    private long scramble(long id) {
        long v = feistel(id);
        while (v >= SPACE) v = feistel(v);   // cycle-walk into the 7-char range
        return v;
    }

    private long feistel(long v) {
        int left  = (int) ((v >>> 21) & MASK21);
        int right = (int) (v & MASK21);
        for (int key : ROUND_KEYS) {
            int next = left ^ roundFunction(right, key);
            left = right;
            right = next;
        }
        return ((long) left << 21) | right;
    }

    private int roundFunction(int x, int key) {
        int h = x ^ key;
        h *= 0x2545F491;
        h ^= h >>> 15;
        h *= 0x2545F491;
        h ^= h >>> 13;
        return h & MASK21;
    }
}

public final class Base62 {
    private static final char[] ALPHABET =
        "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ".toCharArray();
    private static final int BASE = 62;

    public static String encode(long value) {
        if (value == 0) return "0";
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(7);
        long v = value;
        while (v > 0) {
            sb.append(ALPHABET[(int) (v % BASE)]);
            v /= BASE;
        }
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    public static long decode(String code) {
        long value = 0;
        for (char c : code.toCharArray()) {
            value = value * BASE + indexOf(c);
        }
        return value;
    }

    private static int indexOf(char c) {
        if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') return c - '0';
        if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') return c - 'a' + 10;
        if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') return c - 'A' + 36;
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("not base62: " + c);
    }
}
Core point

🔴 Three things to volunteer here, in this order: (1) ranges mean one DB round trip per 10,000 links, not per link; (2) a node crash wastes at most 10k codes out of 3.5 trillion — irrelevant, and the alternative (returning the block) is not worth the complexity; (3) scrambling matters — raw sequential codes let a competitor measure your daily volume by creating two links a day apart, and let anyone enumerate every link in your system.

Trap

⚠️ Why a Feistel network and not "multiply by a large odd number mod 2^n" — the answer most write-ups give, and the one I'd have reached for first.

Two problems with it. First, id * multiplier overflows a 64-bit long for any multiplier large enough to scramble well, and overflow is mod 2⁶⁴, which silently destroys the bijection you were relying on. Second and worse: multiplication by a constant means code(id+1) - code(id) is always the same constant mod N. An attacker creates two links back-to-back, subtracts, recovers the multiplier, and can then enumerate your entire key space — precisely the attack the scramble existed to prevent.

A Feistel network is a permutation by construction (so collisions are impossible, not merely unlikely), has no constant-difference structure, and needs no big-integer arithmetic. This is small-domain format-preserving encryption, and it's the honest answer if the interviewer pushes on "prove two ids can't collide."

Custom aliases

Kept in the same table and same key space as generated codes, with a UNIQUE constraint on the code column:

INSERT INTO links (code, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at)
VALUES (:alias, :url, :owner, now(), :expiry);
-- unique violation -> 409 Conflict. Never SELECT-then-INSERT.

To keep generated codes from ever colliding with aliases, either reserve a prefix/length for aliases (e.g. aliases must be ≥8 chars) or simply let the unique constraint arbitrate and regenerate on the rare clash. Reserving by length is cleaner — it makes collision impossible rather than merely handled.

7. The Read Path — Step by Step

Three details that matter on this path:

  • 302, not 301. A 301 is cached by browsers essentially forever. You would never see the second click from that user — analytics silently dies — and you could never expire or repoint the link. Use 302 (or 307 if you must preserve the method). If asked "isn't 301 better for SEO?", the honest answer is yes for SEO and no for everything else; the business requirement (analytics + mutability) wins.

  • The click event is fire-and-forget. It goes to a bounded in-memory buffer flushed to Kafka in batches. If Kafka is down, you drop click events — you do not fail the redirect. State this trade explicitly: analytics is best-effort, redirect is not.

  • Negative caching. Cache 404s for ~60s. Otherwise a bot scanning random codes drives 100% cache-miss traffic straight to the database — a trivially cheap DoS. This is a genuinely good detail to volunteer.

8. Data Model & Storage

CREATE TABLE links (
    code        VARCHAR(16) PRIMARY KEY,      -- shard key
    long_url    TEXT        NOT NULL,
    owner_id    BIGINT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    expires_at  TIMESTAMPTZ,                  -- NULL = never
    is_disabled BOOLEAN     NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE
);
CREATE INDEX idx_links_owner   ON links (owner_id, created_at DESC);  -- "my links"
CREATE INDEX idx_links_expires ON links (expires_at) WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL;  -- partial

Storage choice — say this comparison:

  • The access pattern is 99% point lookup by primary key. That is a key-value workload, so a wide-column/KV store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) is the natural fit and scales horizontally without effort.

  • But Postgres partitioned by a hash of code handles 115k reads/s behind a 95% cache comfortably — the DB only sees ~6k reads/s. Given you also want the owner_id secondary index and occasional relational queries, start with Postgres and shard by code; move to a KV store when the operational data justifies it.

  • Shard key is code, because every read is by code. owner_id would put all of one user's links together — nice for "my links" but wrong for the 99% path.

Trap

⚠️ The trap: do not add a click_count column and UPDATE it on every redirect. 115k writes/s to a hot row per link, and it puts the database on the redirect path. Counts belong in the analytics pipeline, aggregated from the event stream.

9. Key Design Decisions with Justification

Decision Chosen Rejected Why
Code generation Pre-allocated counter ranges + Base62 + scramble Hash-and-truncate Truncation collides → read-before-write on every create, plus a race.
Code length 7 chars 6 or 8 62⁷ = 3.5T ≈ 96 years of runway at 100M/day. 6 runs out in 18 months.
Sequential leak Bijective scramble Raw counter Sequential codes leak daily volume and allow full enumeration.
Redirect status 302 301 301 is cached forever: kills analytics and makes links immutable.
Read path Cache-first, DB on miss DB-first 100:1 read ratio and a 95% hit rate. The DB is not on the happy path.
Click counting Async event → Kafka → aggregate UPDATE click_count inline 115k writes/s on hot rows would put the DB on the redirect path.
Negative caching Cache 404 for 60s Nothing A code-scanning bot otherwise sends 100% misses to the DB.
Services Read and write deployed separately One service 100:1 traffic ratio, different availability tiers, different scaling curves.
Custom alias collision UNIQUE constraint, catch violation SELECT then INSERT Check-then-act race. Let the DB arbitrate.
Sharding By code By owner_id 99% of queries are point lookups by code.
Expired links 410 Gone, lazy delete + batch sweeper Immediate hard delete 410 is semantically correct, and lazy deletion avoids a delete storm at midnight.

10. Failure Modes & Mitigations

Failure Symptom Mitigation
Redis cluster down All reads fall through to the DB — ~115k/s Read replicas sized to absorb it, plus per-node local LRU (top 10k links) as an L1. Degraded latency, not an outage.
Cache stampede on a viral link One hot code expires; thousands of concurrent misses hit the DB Single-flight/request coalescing per code; jittered TTLs; never expire the top-N links (refresh in background).
Code-scanning bot 100% cache-miss traffic to the DB Negative caching + per-IP rate limiting at the edge.
KGS down Cannot allocate new ranges Each node has up to 10k codes buffered — creates continue for hours. Alert on remaining-block depth, not on KGS liveness.
Two nodes get the same range Duplicate codes Range allocation is a single atomic UPDATE ... RETURNING. The UNIQUE constraint on code is the backstop.
Hot shard One shard saturated Codes are scrambled and hash-partitioned, so distribution is uniform by construction. This is why you scramble.
Malicious / phishing URL Your domain distributes malware Async scan on the write path; a is_disabled flag checked on redirect; blocklist at the edge. Cut from scope but name it.
Kafka down Click events lost Bounded in-memory buffer, then drop. Analytics is best-effort; the redirect must never fail for it.
Redirect loop (someone shortens a short link) Infinite bounce Reject long URLs matching your own domain at create time. Cheap check, embarrassing bug.
DB write of a link, cache not populated First reader takes a miss Acceptable — it's one miss. Do not add a distributed transaction for this.

11. Scale & Cost Considerations

  • Read scaling is mostly free: the redirect service is stateless, so scale horizontally behind an L7 balancer. Add CDN edge caching for the top ~1% of codes and a large slice of traffic never reaches your infrastructure at all.

  • Geographic distribution: links are global, so replicate the Redis cache per region and read from the nearest. Writes go to one primary region — 1.1k writes/s is fine for a single primary, and this keeps you out of multi-leader conflict resolution entirely. Say this: it's an example of choosing the simple consistency model because the write volume permits it.

  • Storage tiering: links older than 2 years with zero clicks in 12 months move to cold storage; the row stays but the payload moves. 22 TB/year makes this a real cost line.

  • Cost intuition: the dominant costs are (a) Redis memory for the hot set, (b) DB storage growth, (c) egress. Compute is nearly free — a redirect is a hash lookup and a header write. If someone asks where the money goes, that's the ranking.

  • The 95% cache hit rate is the load-bearing assumption. Link popularity is strongly Zipfian: a handful of links carry most traffic. If it were uniform, you'd need a far bigger cache or a KV store sized for full traffic. Naming the assumption and what breaks if it's wrong is the senior move.

12. 30-Second Verbal Summary + Follow-up Prep

One-paragraph spoken opener

"This is a 100-to-1 read-heavy system, so I'll design the read path first and treat the write path as almost incidental. Codes are 7-character Base62 — 3.5 trillion combinations, about 96 years of runway at 100 million links a day. I generate them from pre-allocated counter ranges: a key-generation service hands each app node a block of 10,000, so there's no coordination on the hot path and no collisions by construction. I scramble the counter bijectively before encoding, because raw sequential codes leak your daily volume and let anyone enumerate the whole system. Redirects are served from Redis at about a 95% hit rate with the database behind it, returning 302 rather than 301 — a 301 is cached forever, which would kill analytics and make links permanently immutable. Click events are fire-and-forget into Kafka; if that pipeline is down I drop events rather than fail a redirect. And I'd deploy read and write as separate services, since they differ by two orders of magnitude in traffic and have different availability targets."

Follow-up questions to prepare for

Tier 1 — Verifier

  • Why 7 characters? Show me the math.
  • Why 302 and not 301?
  • Why not just hash the URL?
  • What's your read:write ratio and how did it change your design?

Tier 2 — Mechanism

  • Walk me through range allocation when two app nodes start simultaneously.
  • Why scramble the counter? What exactly does an attacker learn without it?
  • A user creates a link and immediately clicks it. Does it work? (→ write-through cache, or read-your-writes from the primary.)
  • How do custom aliases avoid colliding with generated codes?

Tier 3 — Failure modes

  • Redis is entirely down. Walk me through what the user experiences.
  • A link goes viral — 500k requests/s to one code. What breaks first?
  • Someone is scanning random 7-char codes at 50k/s. What happens?
  • KGS has been down for an hour. Can users still create links?

Tier 4 — Open-ended

  • Add per-country, per-referrer analytics with a dashboard. Design that pipeline.
  • Support link expiry at exactly the stated second, globally.
  • Make it multi-region active-active for writes. (→ this is where you'd partition the key space per region so no coordination is needed — each region owns a disjoint range. Good answer.)
  • The product wants to reuse the same short code for the same long URL. What changes? (→ reverse index + dedup on write, and now creates are no longer pure inserts.)

  • DynamoDB / Cassandra instead of sharded Postgres — the workload is genuinely key-value. Simpler to scale, loses the secondary indexes and ad-hoc queries. Offer this as the "if I expect 10× growth" version.

  • Random-code-with-retry instead of ranges — meaningfully simpler (no KGS, no allocator table), and perfectly adequate until the key space is heavily filled. Worth offering as the pragmatic starting point: "I'd ship random-with-retry first and move to ranges when the retry rate becomes measurable."

  • Edge-only architecture (Cloudflare Workers + KV) — the entire redirect path runs at the edge with no origin. Genuinely how a modern small shortener would be built; the trade is vendor lock-in and weaker consistency on writes.

🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why can't you just do SELECT stock ... UPDATE stock in MySQL? Row lock on one hot row serializes all writers; throughput collapses to ~few hundred TPS.
Why does inventory deduction have to be a Lua script, not GET-then-DECR? Redis is single-threaded per command, not per round trip; check-then-act races and oversells.
What fraction of traffic should ever reach the order service? Roughly stock count × 1.2 — everything else is rejected at edge, gateway, or Redis.
What replaces the distributed transaction between order DB and MQ? Transactional outbox (or RocketMQ half-message two-phase commit). Never a bare dual write.
How do you stop a sold-out flash sale from hammering Redis? Local JVM sold-out flag flipped by the Lua return code; short-circuits before the network call.
What closes the loop when a winner never pays? Delay-queue message at T+15min re-checks order status, closes it, and returns stock via compensating increment.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Answer key (cover until tested):

  • A = User browser / mobile client

  • B = Nginx edge (rate limit + static page + CDN origin)

  • C = API gateway (auth, token bucket per user, WAF)

  • D = Seckill service (local limiter, sold-out flag, dedupe)

  • E = Redis Lua script (dedupe + atomic decrement)

  • F = Message queue (order topic, peak shaving)

  • G = Fast rejection response

  • H = Order service consumer (idempotent create)

  • I = Order DB (sharded MySQL) plus outbox table

  • J = Payment service + delay queue for timeout close

  • K = Order confirmed / paid

1. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

  • What's the peak concurrency and how peaky is it? "2M users at exactly 20:00:00" is a fundamentally different system from "200K users over 5 minutes." The former needs edge shedding; the latter is almost a normal service.

  • How many SKUs and how much stock per SKU? One SKU with 10K units is a single hot key problem. 500 SKUs × 20 units is a fan-out problem with much shallower hot keys.

  • Is overselling ever acceptable? Some businesses tolerate over-issuing and refunding (concert merch); others cannot (regulated goods, vaccines, limited-edition with legal SKU count). This single answer decides whether Redis is the source of truth or just a filter.

  • What's the purchase limit rule? One per user per SKU? Per account, per device, per payment instrument, per shipping address? Anti-scalping rules drive the dedupe key design.

  • What's the payment SLA and reservation window? 15 minutes is typical. This determines the delay-queue design and how long stock stays "reserved but unpaid."

  • Is the result allowed to be asynchronous? Can the UI say "you're in the queue, check back" or must it return a definitive order ID synchronously? Synchronous confirmation removes your best peak-shaving lever.

  • Compliance / fairness requirements? Some jurisdictions and some brands require provable FIFO fairness or lottery semantics, which changes the admission mechanism from "first to hit Redis" to "collect entries, draw offline."

2. Functional Requirements

  • Accept purchase attempts for a defined SKU only within the sale window [T_start, T_end]; reject with a distinct code outside it.

  • Enforce a hard inventory ceiling: the count of created orders for a SKU never exceeds its configured stock, under any concurrency.

  • Enforce per-user purchase limits (default: 1 unit per user per SKU per sale).

  • Return a synchronous admission result (ACCEPTED / SOLD_OUT / ALREADY_PARTICIPATED / RATE_LIMITED) in P95 < 150 ms.

  • Create a durable order record asynchronously within 3 seconds of admission, retrievable by orderId and by (userId, skuId).

  • Hold reserved stock for a payment window of 15 minutes; auto-close unpaid orders and return the unit to sellable stock.

  • Support idempotent retries: the same client request token must never produce two orders.

  • Provide an operator console view of sold / reserved / paid / released counts that is accurate within 5 seconds.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

  • Admission latency: P50 < 40 ms, P95 < 150 ms, P99 < 400 ms measured at the gateway.

  • Peak ingress: absorb 500K RPS at the edge for a 30-second burst; deliver no more than ~5K RPS to the seckill service and no more than ~200 RPS of durable writes to the order DB.

  • Correctness: zero oversell — this is a hard invariant, not a target. Under-selling by up to 0.1% (from crashed consumers before compensation runs) is tolerable for one reconciliation cycle.

  • Availability: 99.95% during the sale window. A Redis primary failover must degrade to "sale paused, retry" rather than to oversell.

  • Durability: once a user receives ACCEPTED, the order must eventually exist. No message may be silently dropped between admission and persistence.

  • Isolation of blast radius: flash-sale traffic must not degrade the normal catalog/checkout path — separate Redis cluster, separate MQ topic, separate service pool, separate DB shard group.

  • Observability: per-second time series for admissions, rejections by reason, Redis Lua latency, MQ lag, and order-create success — all with 1-second resolution during the window.

4. High-Level Architecture

The load-bearing idea in this diagram is the funnel: every tier exists to throw away traffic that has no chance of winning, so that the tier below it sees a workload it can actually handle. Edge sheds bots and repeat clickers, gateway sheds per-user floods, the local limiter sheds beyond what the JVM can process, Redis sheds everyone past the stock count, and only the survivors — roughly stock × 1.2 requests — ever touch durable storage.

5. Component-by-Component Breakdown

Static page + CDN

  • What it does: Serves the sale landing page, product images, and countdown JS entirely from CDN edge; the page polls a tiny JSON status endpoint rather than the app.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: Server-rendering the sale page was rejected — at 2M concurrent viewers the rendering alone dwarfs the ordering work, and none of it is user-specific. The rejected alternative (SSR with a Redis-backed page cache) still burns app-tier connections.

  • Key config decisions: Countdown driven by a server timestamp fetched once, then client-side clock; randomized jitter of 0–800 ms on the enable moment to smear the thundering herd.

Nginx edge

  • What it does: Leaky-bucket rate limit keyed on $binary_remote_addr, plus WAF rules and a bot score header.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: Rejecting at Nginx costs ~microseconds and zero JVM threads. A cloud WAF-only approach was rejected because per-IP burst shaping there is coarser and costs per request.

  • Key config decisions: limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=seckill:20m rate=10r/s; with limit_req zone=seckill burst=5 nodelay; and limit_req_status 429. Use limit_req_dry_run on during load tests so you can measure what would have been rejected before enforcing.

API gateway

  • What it does: Validates the JWT, resolves userId, applies a per-user distributed token bucket, and attaches a request token for idempotency.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: Per-IP limiting alone is defeated by NAT (a whole office shares one IP) and by proxy pools. Per-user limiting is the one that actually maps to the business rule. Rejected: doing this in the seckill service, which wastes a service hop for traffic that is definitionally invalid.

  • Key config decisions: 5 requests per user per 10-second window; return 429 with Retry-After. Also enforce the sale window here so pre-sale traffic never reaches the app.

Seckill service (admission)

  • What it does: Applies a local (in-JVM) rate limiter, checks a local sold-out flag, then calls the Redis Lua script.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: The local limiter is the last defense that costs no network. The sold-out flag is the highest-leverage optimization in the whole design — once Lua returns "sold out," this instance flips a boolean and every subsequent request short-circuits without touching Redis. Rejected: relying only on Redis, which means 500K RPS of pointless Redis calls after the stock is gone.

  • Key config decisions: Resilience4j RateLimiter sized at ~2× measured per-instance Redis throughput. Sold-out flag with a 3-second TTL so a stock top-up is picked up quickly.

Redis + Lua (inventory authority during the sale)

  • What it does: One atomic script performs dedupe-check, stock-check, decrement, and participant-set insert, returning a status code.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: MySQL row-level locking on a single stock row serializes every writer and caps you in the hundreds of TPS. Redis WATCH/MULTI optimistic transactions were rejected — under this contention the retry storm is worse than the lock. Lua gives one round trip and true atomicity because Redis executes the whole script without interleaving.

  • Key config decisions: Ship the script via SCRIPT LOAD and call EVALSHA; pass every key explicitly in KEYS so the script is cluster-safe. Preheat stock keys minutes before T_start. Shard hot SKUs into N stock keys (see Section 9).

-- KEYS[1] = stock key shard, KEYS[2] = participant set key
-- ARGV[1] = userId, ARGV[2] = participant TTL seconds
-- returns: 1 = accepted, 0 = sold out, -1 = already participated
if redis.call('SISMEMBER', KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) == 1 then
  return -1
end
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
if stock <= 0 then
  return 0
end
redis.call('DECR', KEYS[1])
redis.call('SADD', KEYS[2], ARGV[1])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[2], tonumber(ARGV[2]))
return 1
Wrong instinct

❌ Wrong design instinct: "I'll GET the stock, check it in Java, then DECR — Redis is single-threaded so it's safe."

✅ Better: Redis is single-threaded per command, not per client round trip. Two clients can both GET a stock of 1 before either DECRs. The atomicity boundary must contain the check and the write — that is exactly what a Lua script (or a DECR-and-compensate pattern) buys you.

Message queue (peak shaving + decoupling)

  • What it does: Carries an OrderIntent message from admission to durable order creation.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: This converts a 500K-RPS spike into a steady 200-RPS drain against the DB — the queue is the shock absorber. Rejected: writing the order synchronously, which pushes DB connection-pool exhaustion into the user's critical path.

  • Key config decisions: Partition by userId hash so a user's messages are ordered. Producer must be reliable — either RocketMQ transactional (half-message) send or a local outbox row written in the same transaction as the Redis-confirmed intent log.

Order service (idempotent consumer)

  • What it does: Consumes OrderIntent, writes the order row, writes the outbox row in the same DB transaction, publishes downstream events.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: Idempotency via a unique index on (userId, skuId, saleId) is cheaper and more reliable than a distributed lock. Rejected: Redis-based distributed lock around order creation — it adds a failure mode (lock expiry mid-write) to solve a problem the database already solves for free.

  • Key config decisions: Catch duplicate-key violation and treat it as success. Consumer group sized so total write concurrency stays under the DB's healthy connection budget.

Payment + delay queue

  • What it does: Handles the payment callback; a delay message fires at T+15min to close unpaid orders and return stock.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: A delay/scheduled message is precise per order. Rejected: a cron job scanning WHERE status='UNPAID' AND created_at < ..., which does a full range scan on your hottest table exactly when it's busiest.

  • Key config decisions: The close operation must be a compensating transaction — mark order CLOSED, INCR the Redis stock shard, and remove the user from the participant set only if business rules allow a retry.

Reconciler

  • What it does: Sweeps the outbox for un-forwarded rows, and periodically audits Redis stock + open orders + paid orders == configured stock.

  • Why this choice over alternatives: This is your safety net against every partial-failure path. It's what turns "probably consistent" into "provably reconciled," and it's the component junior candidates forget.

  • Key config decisions: Run every 30 seconds during the window, every 5 minutes after. Alert — don't auto-correct — on any stock-identity mismatch; auto-correction can mask a real oversell bug.

6. Data Flow — Step by Step

Prose walkthrough:

  1. The client already has the page from CDN; the only dynamic call is the admission POST carrying a client-generated reqToken used for idempotency across retries.

  2. Nginx applies the leaky bucket. Rejections here are the cheapest in the system and should be the largest bucket in your rejection-reason histogram.

  3. The gateway authenticates and applies the per-user bucket. This is where scalpers with one account and many IPs get caught, and where the sale-window check lives.

  4. The seckill service checks its local flag first. Post-sellout, this path never leaves the JVM — that's how you keep Redis alive for the tail of the burst.

  5. The Lua script runs. It is the only place inventory truth is mutated during the sale, and it is atomic, so the oversell invariant holds by construction.

  6. On acceptance, the service sends OrderIntent and returns 202 immediately. Note the ordering hazard: Redis is already decremented but the order does not exist yet. If the MQ send fails, the service must compensate (INCR the shard, remove from participant set) and log to the intent table for the reconciler.

  7. The order consumer writes the order and the outbox row in one local transaction. Duplicate-key violation means a redelivered message — swallow it and ack.

  8. The client polls (or receives a push) using reqToken and gets the orderId, then proceeds to payment. If payment doesn't land in 15 minutes, the delay message closes the order and returns the unit.

7. Key Design Decisions with Justification

Decision Choice Why (and what was rejected)
Inventory authority during sale Redis with Lua script Rejected MySQL UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE qty>0 — correct but the single-row lock serializes writers at ~500 TPS. Rejected WATCH/MULTI — retry storms under extreme contention.
Order creation timing Asynchronous via MQ Rejected synchronous DB insert — couples user latency to DB write capacity and turns a traffic spike into connection-pool exhaustion. Cost: the UI must handle a pending state.
Producer reliability Transactional message or outbox Rejected bare dual write (write DB then send MQ) — a crash between the two silently loses orders. The outbox makes the send derivable from committed DB state.
Duplicate suppression Unique index (userId, skuId, saleId) + Redis participant set Rejected distributed lock — adds lock-expiry failure modes. The Redis set is the fast path; the DB index is the correctness backstop.
Hot key handling Shard stock into N sub-keys, route by hash(userId) % N Rejected a single stock key — one Redis slot becomes the bottleneck and one node's CPU caps the whole sale. Cost: fragmentation (see Section 9).
Unpaid order cleanup Per-order delay message Rejected a scanning cron job — full range scan on the hottest table at the worst moment.
Consistency model Eventual, with a reconciler Rejected 2PC/XA across order, inventory, and payment — resource locking across services collapses concurrency, which is the one thing this system cannot give up.

9. Scale Considerations

Stateless tiers (Nginx, gateway, seckill service). Horizontally scalable, but pre-scale before the window — autoscaling reacts in minutes and the burst lasts seconds. The first thing that breaks is usually connection setup, not compute: TLS handshakes at 500K RPS will exhaust ephemeral ports and CPU before your business logic does. Terminate TLS at the edge with session resumption, and keep persistent connections from gateway to app.

Redis (the real bottleneck). A single primary handles roughly 80–120K ops/s for a small Lua script. At 10x load, one stock key on one slot is your ceiling. Shard the SKU into N keys (stock:{sku}:0..N-1) sized so each shard holds total_stock / N and route by hash(userId) % N. The cost is fragmentation: shard 3 can be empty while shard 7 still has units, producing a false sold-out. Mitigate with a cheap fallback — on a 0 return, retry once against (shard + 1) % N before declaring sold out, and cap N at roughly total_stock / 50 so no shard is thin.

Message queue. Partition count sets your max consumer parallelism. Partitioning by userId hash preserves per-user ordering and spreads load; partitioning by skuId does not (one SKU is the whole sale). At 100x, the queue depth is fine — it's designed to buffer — but watch retention: if consumers fall an hour behind and retention is 30 minutes, you lose orders. Set retention generously for sale days.

Order DB. Shard by userId so both the write path and the "my orders" read path hit one shard. Rejected sharding by skuId — one flash-sale SKU would concentrate every write on a single shard, recreating the hot spot you just escaped. The (userId, skuId, saleId) unique index is the invariant enforcer, so it must live inside the shard key's scope.

What breaks first, in order. (1) Nginx worker connections / TLS at ~300–500K RPS per pool. (2) The single Redis slot at ~100K ops/s. (3) MQ producer send latency once broker page cache is exceeded. (4) Order DB connection pool at a few hundred concurrent writes. Every one of these has a specific number you should be able to quote.

11. Cost Optimization Levers

  • Push everything static to CDN — the sale page, images, and countdown script account for the overwhelming majority of bytes and requests. Serving them from origin is the single most expensive mistake available.

  • Local sold-out flag — cuts post-sellout Redis traffic by 95%+, which is what lets you size the Redis cluster for the first second rather than for the full 60.

  • Scale down immediately after the window — the whole cost model is "rent a lot of capacity for one hour." Automate the scale-down; forgotten pre-scaled fleets are the real budget leak.

  • Reuse one shared seckill cluster across campaigns — per-sale isolation via key namespacing and MQ topics rather than per-sale infrastructure.

  • Reject as early as possible, always — every tier a doomed request penetrates costs strictly more than the tier above. Rejection cost ordering: CDN < Nginx < gateway < JVM < Redis < MQ < DB, roughly an order of magnitude per hop.

  • Batch the order inserts — draining the queue with batched multi-row inserts (100 rows per transaction) cuts DB IOPS by ~10x versus row-at-a-time, at the cost of coarser failure granularity.

One-paragraph spoken opener

The first thing I'd monitor is the gap between Redis decrements and orders created — that's where undersell hides. Follow-up Questions to Prepare For

Tier 1 — Verifier

How do you actually prove you didn't oversell?

The invariant is an accounting identity, and I'd assert it continuously rather than trusting the code path. For a given sale, configured_stock must always equal redis_remaining + orders_open + orders_paid + orders_closed_pending_release. A reconciler evaluates this every 30 seconds during the window and every 5 minutes afterward.

If it ever fails, that's a page, not an auto-correction. Auto-healing a stock mismatch is tempting and wrong — it papers over the bug that caused it, and on the next sale you'll oversell without ever knowing why. The reconciler reports; a human decides.

I'd also run this as a load test assertion, not just a production monitor. The test harness fires 50K concurrent virtual users at 100 units of stock and asserts exactly 100 orders exist. That test catches the check-then-act regression that someone will inevitably introduce when they "optimize" the Lua script into two round trips.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Walk me through what happens if Redis decrements successfully but the MQ send fails.

At that instant the system has taken a unit out of sellable inventory with no order to show for it — an undersell in progress. The seckill service catches the send failure and runs a compensating action: INCR the same stock shard and SREM the user from the participant set, then returns a retryable error to the client.

Compensation itself can fail — the process can be killed between the failed send and the INCR. So before touching Redis at all, the service writes a short-lived intent record (either a local durable log or a Redis key with the reqToken). The reconciler sweeps intents older than 60 seconds that have neither a matching order nor a recorded compensation, and releases them.

This is why the design uses a transactional outbox or RocketMQ's half-message protocol on the order-service side: it removes the equivalent dual-write hazard one layer down. The general principle I'd state out loud is that any place where two systems must change together needs either a two-phase protocol or a compensation-plus-sweeper — never a bare sequential write with a hopeful try/catch.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

It's 20:00:03, the sale is live, and Redis P99 just went from 2ms to 900ms. What do you do?

First I'd check whether it's saturation or a slow script. The distinguishing signal is INFO commandstats for evalsha versus overall instantaneous_ops_per_sec — if ops are flat at ~100K and latency is climbing, I'm CPU-bound on one slot, which given the numbers in Section 9 is the expected first failure. If ops dropped while latency rose, something is blocking: an unintended KEYS scan, an RDB fork, or a slow script someone shipped.

The immediate mitigation is to lean harder on the tiers above. Tighten the gateway token bucket, drop the local limiter's permits, and confirm the sold-out flag is actually flipping — a bug where the flag never sets is a common cause of exactly this symptom, because the whole post-sellout tail keeps hitting Redis. That's a config push, not a deploy.

The structural fix for the next sale is shard count. With a single stock key I have one slot's CPU and nothing else; with N = total_stock / 50 shards the same load spreads across the cluster. I'd also pre-warm and pre-load the script with SCRIPT LOAD before the window, because a NOSCRIPT storm at T+0 turns every request into a full script transmission.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Redesign this for 500 concurrent flash sales instead of one, running continuously.

The bottleneck moves from Redis CPU to configuration and isolation. One SKU with a 100K-ops/s hot key becomes 500 SKUs each doing 200 ops/s — that's an easy Redis workload. The hard part is that a runaway sale must not starve the other 499, so I'd add per-sale quotas at the gateway (each saleId gets a share of the global admission budget) and per-sale MQ topics or at minimum per-sale partition keys, so one campaign's consumer lag doesn't block another's.

The components mostly compose unchanged, but two things become first-class that were incidental before. Sale configuration becomes a real control plane — schedules, stock, limits, and enable/disable, all pushed to services with a short TTL cache so an operator can kill one campaign in seconds. And the reconciler goes from a single-sale assertion to a batch job over all active sales, which means the stock identity check needs an index-friendly shape rather than a full scan.

The cost risk inverts. For one big sale you rent a huge fleet for an hour; for 500 continuous sales you're paying for steady capacity, and idle-hour waste dominates. I'd size for aggregate steady state with burst headroom rather than for any single peak, and I'd expect the CDN and edge tier — not Redis or the DB — to be the largest line item, because the page traffic scales with campaigns while the ordering work stays small.
